Cisco (CSCO) crashed 87% after its March 2000 peak and needed until December 2025 to close higher, despite a business that kept growing.

Nvidia (NVDA), today's AI picks-and-shovels leader, trades at roughly 37 times earnings versus Cisco's peak multiple above 200, yet its shares have still fallen 21% in a month.

Great companies bought at peak multiples can deliver poor returns for decades, so the price paid for AI growth matters as much as the growth.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Although Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) has spent 2026 riding a fresh wave of AI networking orders, Wall Street still measures the company against one trading day from the dot-com era. At the close on Monday, March 27, 2000, the Associated Press reported, Cisco had a market value of $555.5 billion on basic shares. That inched past Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) at $541.6 billion and made Cisco the world's most valuable company. Sherwood News reporter Matt Phillips put Cisco's dot-com closing high at $80.06. But buyers who paid that price waited more than 25 years for a higher close, Matt Phillips found. That history matters again now, because the biggest tech selloff in years has shaken the AI companies that hold Cisco's old crown.

Justin Sullivan / Getty Images
How Cisco Got Priced for Perfection

Cisco sold the picks and shovels of the internet boom. Its routers and switches carried the traffic of the dot-com expansion, and Matt Phillips reported that its stock vaulted roughly 4,000% from the end of 1994 to March 2000. By the peak, investors were paying in advance for decades of perfect growth. Per the Financial Times, as summed up by Slashdot, Cisco traded at a price-to-earnings ratio above 200 and an enterprise value-to-sales ratio of 31.

title: This Is the Best-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026. Is It Still a Buy?
detail:
This Is the Best-Performing Magnificent Seven Stock of 2026. Is It Still a Buy?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

^GSPC

Trading disclosure

The "Magnificent Seven" is a grouping of stocks used to describe some of the largest companies in the world that have helped lead the U.S. stock market higher over the past decade. It is made up of:

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL)

Nvidia

Microsoft

Alphabet

Amazon

Meta Platforms

Tesla

For U.S.-listed stocks, all seven of these are in the top 10, so being on this list is a big deal. However, 2026 hasn't been the greatest year for the Magnificent Seven. The S&P 500 is up about 12.3% this year, and only three stocks are outperforming it: Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft. But which one of these is doing the best? It's the non-AI one.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Apple leads all Magnificent Seven stocks

The top performer so far in 2026 has been Apple, up about 29%. That's practically double the second-best performer, Amazon, which has risen around 15%. So, what has separated Apple from the competition? I think there are two reasons.

First, Apple really isn't an AI stock. While its products have some AI features, it's not spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers like every other company on this list (besides Nvidia, which is selling the equipment for these data centers). As a whole, the market has been a bit bearish on the AI buildout lately, and Apple has been a haven for investors who aren't as keen on the long-term prospects of AI.

In fact, Apple is the only stock among the top 10 largest companies on U.S. exchanges that doesn't have significant AI investments or business cases riding on the AI buildout. This has made it a safe haven for non-AI investors and has boosted its stock.

Another reason Apple has done well this year is that its iPhone 17 lineup was the most popular of any of its previous models. This has driven sales growth and has made Apple a respectable business again.

However, Apple's day of reckoning could be coming. Outside of Tesla (which has a sky-high valuation of 424 times trailing earnings), Apple is by far the most expensive stock in the Magnificent Seven.

NVDA PE Ratio data by YCharts

As a result, I think the stock could be getting a bit too pricey, and investors need to watch out. Apple's strong performance this year hasn't come entirely from business results, and if the market flips its stance on AI and becomes bullish on it again, Apple's stock could sell off in favor of some AI-focused investments. It's about as good as it gets for Apple sentiment right now. As a result, I don't think Apple stock is a buy right now.

title: Microsoft Is Reportedly Getting Pickier About AI Data Center Deals. Is the Stock a Buy Now?

Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool

NBIS

Trading disclosure

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) might be getting choosier about where its artificial intelligence (AI) computing power comes from.

On Nov. 5, Bloomberg said that the software giant has tightened oversight of some projects from neoclouds (firms that rent out AI computing capacity), including Nebius Group, IREN (NASDAQ:IREN), and the privately held Nscale. Microsoft is backing away from projects it finds risky, according to the report. And the Financial Times reported the same day that Microsoft won't exercise an option to more than double the size of its Nscale deal at a Texas data center. Microsoft hasn't confirmed either report.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

IREN said on Nov. 5 that a customer-requested design change and vendor timing pushed its goal of over $4 billion in annualized revenue into early 2027. Its quarterly filing says Microsoft asked for a network design change across the deployments IREN is delivering under their agreement.

The stock trades near $535 as of this writing, about 4% below its Nov. 4 record close of $555.80. A slower pace of outside deals may sound like relief for Microsoft's shrinking free cash flow. I'm not sure it is.

Image source: Getty Images.

Free cash flow is still falling

Microsoft's spending has climbed far faster than the cash its business brings in. During its fiscal 2027 first quarter (which ended Sept. 30, 2026), cash from operations rose 29% year over year to $58 billion. But cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4 billion, more than twice the year-ago amount.

Sure, adjusted earnings per share still grew 18% year over year for the quarter.

Free cash flow (cash from operations minus cash spent on property and equipment) is another story. It was around $60 billion over the last four reported quarters, down from about $67 billion for fiscal 2026 and about $78 billion in the four quarters ended September 2025. That's a fall of about 23%, and the decline hasn't stopped.

"To complement cash generated by the business and preserve financial flexibility, we will access additional sources of funding when we believe it is attractive to do so," CFO Amy Hood said on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call on Oct. 28.

A day later, Microsoft agreed to sell $25 billion in notes.

Would renting less help?

Chip stocks took the brunt of the damage, with AI chip designers and memory makers among the hardest hit. The slide erased the gains from a day earlier, when the Dow had jumped 3% for its best session of 2026 after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Yahoo Finance wrote on November 4. By mid-session Thursday, the index was heading for its worst second day after a midterm election in data going back to 1896, the outlet noted.

The Dow's Safe-Haven Run Cracks

For most of the week, the Dow had looked like the sheltered corner of the market. Yahoo Finance reported on November 2 that the Dow edged up 0.4% while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 1% as investors rotated out of technology names and into consumer cyclical and financial services shares, which left the Dow looking like the market's relative winner. On Thursday, that cushion gave way, as the focus turned to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI buildout, and for the data centers driving it in particular. The reversal was fast and violent. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at an equity research firm, pointed out that the VIX volatility index posted its biggest one-day jump in more than two years. That Wednesday buying had been helped by falling oil prices, while the Windows maker jumped 6% to a record high.

A Jobs Report Steadies the Tape

Friday brought a partial rebound. Yahoo Finance reported on November 6 that the US added 165,000 jobs in October, and the Nasdaq gained 1.9% while the S&P 500 rose 1% and the Dow added 0.1%. title: 'There's no question about it': Warren Buffett and Bill Gates reveal the same 1-word secret to success

'There's no question about it': Warren Buffett and Bill Gates reveal the same 1-word secret to success

World-renowned billionaires Warren Buffett and Bill Gates built their fortunes in very different industries. But when asked to sum up the secret to their success in just one word, they both gave the exact same answer: focus.

For Gates, that meant an obsession with coding as a teenager that eventually led him to co-found Microsoft. Buffett, meanwhile, developed an early fascination with investing that helped make him one of history's most successful investors.

"He was focused on software, I was focused on investments," Buffett told CNBC (1). "And it gave me a big advantage to start very young — there's no question about it."

Their shared philosophy offers a valuable lesson for everyday investors: Success isn't necessarily about chasing every opportunity. Sometimes, it's about identifying what matters most and tuning out the distractions.

Here are three ways to apply that philosophy to your own investment strategy.

Start early and stay focused

When Buffett was just 11 years old, he invested $114.75 of his savings in three shares of oil and gas company Cities Service. It was the beginning of a lifelong fascination with investing that would eventually help him build a multibillion-dollar fortune.

Buffett has long championed the power of compounding, which allows investment earnings to generate additional earnings over time. He once compared the process to rolling a snowball down a hill.

"We started building this little snowball on top of a very long hill," he said at Berkshire Hathaway's annual shareholders meeting in 1999 (2). "The trick is to have a very long hill, either start very young or live to be very old."

Of course, not everyone starts investing at 11. But even if you're getting a later start, consistently putting money aside can be more productive than waiting for the perfect moment to invest.

And you don't necessarily need a large sum of money to build that habit. In fact, you can start by putting the spare change from everyday purchases to work.

That's where Acorns comes in. The automated investing app helps you stay focused on building wealth by turning ordinary purchases into opportunities to invest, without having to make a new decision every time.
